purpose: Evidence-first pest and disease reference profiles for Teaching Healthy Cultivation. Profiles support identification and differential reasoning; they do not treat a single image or symptom as confirmation.

profiles.title: Spider Mites
profiles.summary: Spider mites are tiny arachnids that feed on plant cells. Early infestations can be easy to miss because damage may appear before obvious webbing.
observe: Fine stippling or pale speckling that expands over time
Mites, eggs, or cast skins on leaf undersides under magnification
Webbing in heavier infestations, often around petioles, leaf edges, or dense growth
Hot or dry microclimates where populations may increase rapidly
lookAlikes: Dust or residue mistaken for eggs or cast skins
confirm: Inspect several symptomatic and nearby leaves with magnification
Look for moving mites plus eggs rather than webbing alone
Map distribution and repeat counts to determine whether the population is increasing
riskContext: Dense canopies can hide early colonies
New plants, clothing, tools, and nearby vegetation can move pests between areas
Environmental conditions can influence population growth but do not prove mite presence
managementPrinciples: Isolate affected material when practical and prevent movement to clean areas
Remove heavily damaged or infested debris according to site policy
Improve scouting frequency and preserve before/after counts
Use only lawful, label-compliant biological, cultural, mechanical, or chemical controls appropriate to the crop and location

profiles.title: Thrips
profiles.summary: Thrips are slender insects whose feeding can create silvery scars, distorted young growth, and dark fecal specks. Several life stages may occur in different parts of the crop environment.
observe: Silvery or bronze feeding scars rather than uniform chlorosis
Small elongated insects on leaves, flowers, or traps
Dark fecal specks associated with feeding sites
Distorted or scarred new growth when feeding occurs on developing tissue
confirm: Use magnification to identify body shape and movement
Inspect sticky cards and plant tissue together
Check more than one life stage when possible and track repeated counts
riskContext: Incoming plant material can introduce thrips
Flowers and protected growing points can shelter insects
Weeds or nearby vegetation can serve as alternate hosts
managementPrinciples: Quarantine and inspect incoming plants
Use repeatable trap and plant-scouting routes
Reduce unnecessary plant debris and alternate hosts
Use only lawful, crop-appropriate, label-compliant controls and verify the result with follow-up counts

profiles.title: Fungus Gnats
profiles.summary: Adult fungus gnats are small flies often associated with moist organic substrates. Larvae develop in the root zone and can feed on organic matter, fungi, and tender roots.
observe: Small dark adults running or flying near the media surface
Larvae in moist media under close inspection
Persistent wet media or algae/fungal growth that supports larval habitat
Weak young plants where root injury is plausible
lookAlikes: Seedling problems caused by overwatering without meaningful gnat pressure
Root disease unrelated to insect feeding
confirm: Use sticky cards for adult trend data
Inspect the media or use an appropriate larval sampling method
Separate insect presence from proof that insects caused the plant symptom
riskContext: Chronically wet media favors habitat development
Propagation areas can be particularly vulnerable
Algae and decaying organic matter can support populations
managementPrinciples: Correct avoidable overwatering and improve media/aeration practices where appropriate
Remove standing water and unnecessary organic debris
Monitor adults and larvae separately
Use only lawful, crop-appropriate biological or other controls and verify population change

profiles.title: Aphids
profiles.summary: Aphids are soft-bodied sap-feeding insects that may cluster on growing tips, stems, or leaf undersides. Honeydew and cast skins can be important clues.
observe: Clusters of soft-bodied insects in protected plant areas
Sticky honeydew on leaves or surfaces
White cast skins that remain after molting
Curling or distorted young growth in feeding areas
confirm: Identify living insects under magnification
Check stems, petioles, growing points, and leaf undersides
Record colony locations and repeat counts
riskContext: Dense growth can conceal colonies
Winged forms can disperse from established populations
Incoming plant material is a common biosecurity concern
managementPrinciples: Inspect and quarantine incoming material
Remove heavily colonized plant debris where practical
Protect beneficial organisms when using controls
Use only lawful, label-compliant controls and confirm declining counts over time

profiles.title: Whiteflies
profiles.summary: Whiteflies are small sap-feeding insects. Adults may fly when leaves are disturbed, while immature stages remain attached to leaf undersides.
observe: Small pale adults flying from disturbed foliage
Flattened immature stages on leaf undersides
Honeydew and associated surface growth where populations are high
General decline or chlorosis that tracks with infestation intensity
lookAlikes: Scale insects or residue on leaf undersides
confirm: Inspect adults and immature stages
Use sticky cards for trend data, not as the sole identification tool
Check whether symptoms spatially correspond with actual colonies
riskContext: Protected environments can allow continuous reproduction
New plants can introduce hidden immature stages
Honeydew can create secondary cleanliness and microbial concerns
managementPrinciples: Strengthen incoming-plant inspection
Remove heavily infested material where site policy allows
Monitor adult and immature stages separately
Use lawful, crop-appropriate controls and verify population trends

profiles.title: Broad & Russet Mite Suspicion
profiles.summary: Broad and russet mites are extremely small and may cause distorted new growth, bronzing, reduced vigor, or flower damage. Visual symptoms alone are not sufficient for confirmation.
observe: Abnormal distortion concentrated in new growth
Bronzing, roughened tissue, or unusual leaf margins
Symptoms that persist despite otherwise reasonable nutrition and environment
Very small organisms requiring strong magnification or microscopy
confirm: Use suitable magnification or microscopy on symptomatic growing points
Sample more than one plant and location
Consider professional identification when the organism cannot be resolved reliably
riskContext: Symptoms can be severe before mites are noticed
Plant-to-plant movement and contaminated tools/material can spread infestations
Misdiagnosis can lead to repeated unnecessary input changes
managementPrinciples: Isolate suspicious material until identification improves
Strengthen sanitation and movement controls
Preserve samples/photos and repeat scouting
Use lawful, crop-appropriate controls only after the target is reasonably established

profiles.title: Caterpillars & Chewing Larvae
profiles.summary: Caterpillars and other chewing larvae remove tissue directly and can hide inside dense foliage or flowers. Frass is often an important clue.
observe: Missing tissue, holes, or chewed margins
Frass near damaged tissue
Larvae, silk, or feeding shelters
Flower damage that may create secondary decay risk
lookAlikes: Necrotic tissue that later falls away
confirm: Search damaged areas and nearby protected sites
Identify larvae or characteristic frass
Inspect at different times when feeding activity may change
riskContext: Outdoor crops are exposed to egg-laying adults and surrounding vegetation
Dense flowers can hide larvae and damage
Wounds can increase secondary disease concerns
managementPrinciples: Remove confirmed larvae when practical
Use exclusion and repeated scouting where appropriate
Inspect damaged flower tissue for secondary decay
Use lawful, crop-appropriate controls and verify reduced damage/new counts

profiles.title: Powdery Mildew
profiles.summary: Powdery mildew presents as superficial white fungal growth on susceptible tissue. Similar-looking residues make confirmation important before management decisions are made.
observe: White powdery colonies that recur or expand rather than wiping away permanently
Distribution on leaves, petioles, stems, or flowers depending on disease stage
New colonies appearing over time
Microclimates with limited air movement or favorable humidity patterns
confirm: Inspect colony structure with magnification
Compare wiped and unwiped areas over time
Use microscopy or laboratory testing when species-level or regulatory confirmation matters
riskContext: Dense canopies and susceptible cultivars can increase risk
Air movement within the canopy and moisture management affect disease conditions
Infected plant material can serve as inoculum
managementPrinciples: Separate or remove heavily affected material according to site policy
Improve sanitation and environmental management
Reduce movement of contaminated plant debris
Use only lawful, crop-appropriate disease controls and verify new-colony incidence

profiles.title: Botrytis / Gray Mold Suspicion
profiles.summary: Botrytis can infect damaged or senescing tissues and is especially concerning in dense flowering material. Internal decay may be present before the exterior looks severe.
observe: Localized browning, collapse, or soft decay inside flowers
Gray-brown sporulation under favorable conditions
Damage following prolonged wetness, condensation, injury, or dense flower development
Affected tissue that separates from healthy material abnormally
confirm: Inspect the interior of suspicious flower tissue carefully
Document wetness/condensation and progression
Use microscopy or laboratory testing when definitive identification is important
riskContext: Dense flowers can trap moisture
Rain, condensation, and prolonged high moisture increase risk
Wounded or senescing tissues can be vulnerable entry points
managementPrinciples: Isolate affected material and avoid spreading spores/debris
Remove contaminated tissue according to site policy
Address moisture, condensation, and canopy airflow problems
Use lawful, crop-appropriate disease controls and protect post-harvest material from contaminated batches

profiles.title: Root-Zone Disease Complex
profiles.summary: Brown roots, weak growth, wilt, or root loss can result from low oxygen, temperature, salinity, physical injury, pathogens, or combinations of these factors. Root appearance alone rarely identifies the causal organism.
observe: Root color, texture, odor, and distribution of damage
Whether roots are slimy, dry, brittle, stained, or mechanically damaged
Media moisture, drainage, oxygenation, and root-zone temperature
Whole-plant wilt, stunting, or nutrient-like symptoms
lookAlikes: Normal staining from media or nutrient inputs
confirm: Separate environmental/root-zone evidence from pathogen evidence
Compare healthy and symptomatic root samples
Use microscopy, culturing, molecular testing, or a plant diagnostic laboratory when causal identification matters
riskContext: Saturated or poorly aerated zones can damage roots and favor some pathogens
Warm or unstable root-zone conditions can increase stress
Shared water, tools, or reused material can spread some root pathogens
managementPrinciples: Correct physical root-zone problems that can be measured
Separate contaminated material and strengthen sanitation
Avoid assuming every brown root is the same disease
Use lawful, crop-appropriate disease controls only with an evidence-based target

profiles.title: Hop Latent Viroid (HLVd) Suspicion
profiles.summary: Hop latent viroid can infect cannabis and may be associated with reduced vigor, altered morphology, poor rooting, or reduced flower/resin performance. Symptoms are variable and visual inspection cannot confirm infection.
observe: Unexplained loss of vigor or performance across clones or time
Abnormal branching, leaf shape, rooting, or developmental behavior in some infected plants
Patterns associated with shared propagation material
Plants that look normal despite possible infection
confirm: Use a validated molecular diagnostic test such as an appropriate RT-PCR/RT-qPCR assay through a capable laboratory
Sample according to the laboratory's guidance
Do not use visual symptoms as a substitute for testing
riskContext: Vegetative propagation can preserve and spread infected plant material
Contaminated cutting tools or plant sap can create transmission risk
Asymptomatic infected plants can make visual screening unreliable
managementPrinciples: Use tested propagation stock where practical
Strengthen tool sanitation and plant-identity records
Separate suspect material pending test results
Follow applicable facility, laboratory, and crop-health protocols for confirmed infected stock

profiles.title: Damping-Off & Seedling Collapse
profiles.summary: Seedling collapse near the media surface can involve pathogenic fungi or oomycetes, but excessive moisture, poor aeration, weak seedlings, temperature, and mechanical injury can create similar outcomes or increase disease risk.
observe: Stem constriction or water-soaked tissue near the media line
Seedlings that fail before or shortly after emergence
Root discoloration or decay
Clusters associated with wet media, poor airflow, contaminated materials, or propagation trays
lookAlikes: Nutrient or salt injury to very young roots
confirm: Inspect stem/root tissue and compare affected with healthy seedlings
Document propagation moisture, temperature, sanitation, and emergence timing
Use a plant diagnostic laboratory when identification of the causal organism matters
riskContext: Very young plants have limited reserves and small root systems
Saturated media and poor sanitation can increase disease risk
Contaminated trays, tools, water, or media can contribute to repeated outbreaks
managementPrinciples: Use clean propagation materials and tools
Avoid chronically saturated media and maintain appropriate aeration
Remove collapsed seedlings according to sanitation practice
Use lawful, crop-appropriate disease management only when the target and context justify it
